The unavailability of land, increasing urban congestion, higher taxes, and technological advances in power, communications, and transportation have motivated many businesses and manufacturers to seek new sites beyond present commercial zone limits. Many firms have been forced to relocate in the suburbs by urban redevelopment projects and highway construction. This upswing in business activity in the suburbs is not separate from the life of the center city, but rather an inevitable outgrowth of its economic and social development.
The Interim Report summarized the findings of two studies of essentially different urban areas of the country - Philadelphia in the "urban" Northeast and Mississippi in the "rural" South. The Philadelphia study, conducted by the Penjerdel Corporation, revealed that from 1940 to 1970, the population and business activity in the counties surrounding the city increased dramatically and at a much faster rate than in the city itself. It found that the suburbs engage in substantial trade with the city, look to it for professional and commercial services, and are served by the same utility companies. The Mississippi study, conducted by the Mississippi Research and Development Center, demonstrated that during the past 20 years Mississippi has changed from a primarily agricultural to a primarily industrial State. Most new industry is located in industrial parks several miles from the nearest city. These businesses often have difficulty in securing adequate transportation services because they are not located within any existing commercial zone.
